title: Humans tamed the mammoth
premise: Around 12000 BCE herders on the cold northern steppe learn to raise woolly mammoth calves for wool, milk and pulling power. Protected and fed by people, mammoths persist through later climate change and spread with farmers and traders. Their need for fodder, space and wide streets shapes how people farm, travel and build ever after.

chain.event: Steppe foragers capture young mammoths and raise them with reindeer herds for milk and wool
chain.consequence: tame herds live beside people and persist through later climate shifts, giving villages a large source of fiber and pulling power

chain.event: Keepers begin sowing grasses and storing hay in river valleys to feed mammoths through the cold season
chain.consequence: year-round fodder allows larger settled villages with barns and hayfields and steady population growth

chain.event: Carpenters develop heavy wagons and a soil-cutting ard pulled by mammoth teams for plowing and hauling timber and grain
chain.consequence: bulk loads move far overland on wide cleared tracks, linking farms to larger market towns

chain.event: Spinners and weavers turn clipped mammoth underwool into felt and heavy cloth on upright looms
chain.consequence: wool trade supports full-time herders, weavers and long-distance caravan traffic in textiles and salt

chain.event: Breeders select calmer, smaller city mammoths while farmers expand clover and root crops for feed and harness makers improve yokes
chain.consequence: mammoth teams stay cheap and reliable for farms and city haulage, slowing the shift to fuel engines for heavy work

chain.event: Town councils keep wide mammoth avenues, paddocks and water troughs while adding buried electric lines and piped water
chain.consequence: modern growth stays low and spread out around animal streets, entering 2026 with mixed mammoth and electric transport

eras.caption: 26 · wide lanes between low barns and houses
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 26 in a world where humans tamed the mammoth. Low houses in the region's own building tradition stand apart with large fodder barns and haystacks, and a very wide packed-earth lane carries mammoth teams and heavy sledges.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: Show a low interior room with thick walls, small windows, woven mammoth-wool blankets and felt hangings, lit by oil lamps.

differences: low scattered one-story houses with large yards instead of compact dense rows (because each household keeps standing room and feed for mammoths)
very wide packed-earth lanes instead of narrow foot paths (because paired mammoth teams need room to pass and turn)
large timber-and-earth fodder barns and haystacks beside homes instead of small grain bins (because bulky cold-season feed is stored at the house)
mammoth-drawn sledges and heavy wagons instead of donkey carts and human porters (because bulk hauling is done by domestic mammoths)
woven mammoth-wool felt fences and awnings instead of plain reed mats (because clipped underwool is plentiful and worked locally)
kept: house forms in the region's own building tradition

broad level earth avenues with troughs and hitching posts instead of narrow cobbled lanes (because daily movement is by large draft animals)

outer hayfields and winter paddocks reaching to the houses instead of tight suburbs (because town mammoths are fed and rested close by)

hand looms, pottery and market gardens
